lessons.title: Types of Raw Materials: Silica, Soda Ash, Limestone
lessons.body: Glass is made from three main raw materials: silica sand, soda ash, and limestone. In Africa, silica sand is often mined locally from riverbeds or beaches. For good glass, you need sand with at least 95% silica (SiO2) and low iron (below 0.1% Fe2O3) to avoid green or brown tint. A simple field test: put a spoonful of sand in a clear bottle with water, shake, and let settle. If the water stays clear, iron is low. Soda ash (sodium carbonate, Na2CO3) lowers the melting point of silica from about 1700Â°C to around 1400Â°C, saving fuel. It is often imported from Kenya or South Africa in 50 kg bags. Limestone (calcium carbonate, CaCO3) adds calcium oxide, which makes glass more durable and resistant to water. You need about 10-15% limestone in the batch. In many African countries, limestone is quarried locally, like in Nigeria or Tanzania. A typical batch recipe by weight: 70% silica sand, 15% soda ash, 10% limestone, and 5% cullet (recycled glass). But this varies with local sand purity. Always test your materials: burn a small sample in a kiln to see melting behaviour. If the melt is too thick, add more soda ash; if it cracks easily, add more limestone. Store each material separately in dry, labelled bins. Moisture makes soda ash clump and ruins weighing. Use a simple moisture meter or dry a sample in an oven at 110Â°C for 2 hours to check. Remember, consistency is key: same source, same ratio, every time.

lessons.title: Cullet: Sources, Benefits, and Preparation
lessons.body: Cullet is broken or waste glass that you add back into the batch. In Africa, good sources are bottle banks, local bars, hotels, and glass factories. You can also buy cullet from recyclers in cities like Nairobi, Lagos, or Accra. Using cullet saves money: it melts at a lower temperature (about 1200Â°C) than raw materials, cutting fuel use by up to 30%. It also reduces the need for soda ash and limestone. A typical batch can include 20-50% cullet, but you must prepare it properly. First, sort by colour: clear, green, and brown cullet must be kept separate because mixed colours give dirty glass. Remove all contaminants: caps, labels, ceramics, stones, and metals. Ceramics are the worstâeven a small piece can cause stones or cracks in the final product. Crush cullet to a uniform size, about 10-20 mm, using a hammer mill or a manual pestle. Wash it to remove dust, sugar residue, and dirt. Dry it in the sun or in a dryer. Store cullet in dry, covered bins. If you use too much cullet, the glass may become brittle because some oxides are lost. A safe rule: keep cullet below 50% unless you add extra soda ash. Test each batch: melt a small sample and check for bubbles or seeds. In rural areas, womenâs groups often collect and crush cullet as a business. You can train them to sort and clean properly. Always wear gloves and eye protection when handling culletâsharp edges cut deep.

lessons.title: Batch Calculation and Mixing Procedures
lessons.body: Batch calculation means working out exactly how much of each raw material to weigh for a given amount of glass. You need a simple formula based on the chemical composition of your materials. For example, if your sand is 98% silica, soda ash 58% Na2O, and limestone 56% CaO, you calculate the required weights to get a target glass composition. A typical target for container glass: 72% SiO2, 12% Na2O, 10% CaO, 1% Al2O3, and 5% other. Letâs say you want 100 kg of glass. You need 72 kg SiO2. If sand is 98% pure, weigh 72 / 0.98 = 73.5 kg sand. For Na2O, you need 12 kg. Soda ash is 58% Na2O, so weigh 12 / 0.58 = 20.7 kg. For CaO, 10 kg needed; limestone is 56% CaO, so weigh 10 / 0.56 = 17.9 kg. Add 5 kg cullet (or more, adjusting other materials). Total batch weight = 73.5 + 20.7 + 17.9 + 5 = 117.1 kg. This gives 100 kg of glass because gases escape during melting. Mixing: first weigh each material separately on a scale accurate to 0.1 kg. Then mix dry in a concrete mixer or by hand on a clean floor. Add a little water (2-3%) to reduce dust and prevent segregation. Mix for at least 5 minutes until the colour is uniform. Never mix different batches in the same mixer without cleaning. Keep a logbook: date, batch number, weights, and any changes. This helps you trace defects. In small African workshops, a digital scale and a shovel are enough. Train one person to be responsible for weighingâaccuracy is critical.

lessons.title: Weighing and Blending Equipment
lessons.body: To make good glass, you need reliable weighing and blending equipment. For weighing, a digital platform scale with a capacity of 100-200 kg and accuracy of 0.1 kg is ideal. In many African workshops, you can buy a used scale from a hardware store in Nairobi or Johannesburg for around $200. Always calibrate it weekly with a known weight (e.g., 20 kg bag of cement). For small batches, a kitchen scale up to 5 kg works. Never guessâwrong weights cause defects like cords, stones, or bubbles. For blending, a concrete mixer (tumbler type) is common. A 200-litre mixer can handle 100-150 kg of batch. If you donât have a mixer, mix on a clean concrete floor using shovels: spread materials in layers, then turn the pile three times. Add water slowly (2-3% by weight) using a watering can to control dust. Mix until no streaks of colour remainâusually 5-10 minutes. For larger operations, a ribbon blender or paddle mixer gives better homogeneity. You also need storage bins for each raw material: labelled, dry, and off the ground. Use hoppers with gates for easy feeding. A simple vibratory screen (5 mm mesh) removes lumps before mixing. In rural areas, a hand-cranked mixer can be made from a drum with internal blades. Always wear dust masks when handling soda ash and limestoneâthey irritate lungs. Keep equipment clean: leftover batch in a mixer will contaminate the next mix. After each batch, run the mixer empty for 2 minutes to self-clean. Record equipment maintenance: grease bearings monthly, check belts weekly.

lessons.title: Batch Homogeneity and Quality Control
lessons.body: Batch homogeneity means every scoop of the mixed batch has the same proportion of ingredients. If not, you get defects: streaks, bubbles, or weak glass. To test homogeneity, take 5 samples from different parts of the mixed batch (top, bottom, four corners). Put each in a separate small crucible and melt in a furnace at 1400Â°C for 30 minutes. Cool and examine: all samples should look identical in colour and clarity. If one is different, your mixing is poor. Another simple test: put a handful of batch in water. Soda ash dissolves, sand sinks, limestone floats slightly. If you see layers, mix more. Quality control also includes checking raw material moisture. Weigh a sample, dry at 110Â°C for 2 hours, reweigh. If moisture is above 1%, adjust your batch weight. For soda ash, moisture above 0.5% means you need to add more. Test cullet for ceramics: crush a sample, put in water, ceramics sink faster than glass. Use a magnet to remove iron. Keep a daily log: batch number, mixer time, moisture, and melting results. In African settings, a simple visual check after melting is powerful. Also, check the final glass for seeds (bubbles) and stones (unmelted particles). If you see many seeds, your batch may have too much sulphate or moisture. If stones, your sand is too coarse or mixing is poor. Train workers to spot defects early. A small kiln for test melts costs about $500 and saves thousands in wasted production.

lessons.title: Storage and Handling of Raw Materials
lessons.body: Proper storage keeps raw materials dry, clean, and safe. Silica sand: store in a covered shed or silo on a concrete floor. If stored outdoors, cover with a tarpaulin. Wet sand clumps and gives wrong weights. Soda ash: very hygroscopicâabsorbs moisture from air. Keep in sealed 50 kg bags on pallets, in a dry room. Once opened, use within one week or reseal in airtight containers. Limestone: store like sand, but keep separate to avoid mixing. Cullet: store in covered bins by colour. Never store cullet with raw materialsâsharp pieces can contaminate. All storage areas should be labelled clearly: âSILICA SAND â 98% SiO2â etc. Use first-in, first-out (FIFO) to avoid old stock. Handling: always wear personal protective equipment (PPE): dust mask, safety glasses, gloves, and steel-toe boots. Soda ash dust irritates eyes and lungs; limestone dust is also harmful. Use a shovel with a long handle to avoid bending. For heavy bags, use a trolley or two-person lift. Keep floors sweptâspilled soda ash becomes slippery when wet. In African workshops, a simple wooden pallet and a plastic sheet can protect materials from ground moisture. Check stock weekly: look for caking, mould, or pest damage. If soda ash is caked, break it up and dry it before weighing. Record inventory: date received, quantity, supplier. Train all workers on safe handling. A clean, organised store reduces waste and accidents, and ensures consistent glass quality.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Raw Materials & Batch Preparation for Glass Processing

This practical reference module is designed for African glass processors, from small-scale recyclers in Nairobi's industrial zones to container plants in Egypt and South Africa. Whether you are running a 5-tonne/day tableware furnace or a 200-tonne/day container line, the cost of your batch is dominated by raw materials. In most African markets, raw materials represent 50â65% of total production cost, and cullet availability, transport logistics, and currency fluctuations make sourcing a strategic business function, not just a technical one.

This lesson gives you the numbers, procedures, and quality benchmarks you need to buy smarter, blend consistently, and reduce furnace energy consumption. It is written for the plant manager, batch house supervisor, and procurement officer who need actionable data.

1. Types of Raw Materials: Silica, Soda Ash, Limestone

Glass is primarily silica (SiOâ), fluxed with soda ash (NaâCOâ) to lower melting temperature, and stabilised with limestone (CaCOâ) to improve chemical durability. In Africa, silica sand is available in Egypt (Abu Zenima), Nigeria (Igbokoda), Kenya (Lamu), and South Africa (Cape Flats), but quality varies. Soda ash is largely imported from Kenya's Lake Magadi (Tata Chemicals) or from Turkey, China, and the USA. Limestone is widely sourced locally.

Table 1: Typical Raw Material Specifications for Soda-Lime-Silica Glass
Raw Material Key Oxide Typical Purity Critical Impurities (max) African Sourcing Notes
Silica Sand SiOâ â¥ 99.0% 98.5â99.5% FeâOâ < 0.05%, AlâOâ < 0.5% Egypt, Nigeria, Kenya, South Africa; wash and screen locally to reduce freight.
Soda Ash NaâCOâ â¥ 99.0% 99.0â99.8% NaCl < 0.3%, FeâOâ < 0.003% Lake Magadi, Kenya (Tata Chemicals) supplies East Africa; West Africa imports.
Limestone CaCOâ â¥ 97.0% 96.0â99.0% FeâOâ < 0.1%, MgO < 1.0% Local quarries in Nigeria, Kenya, South Africa; grind to < 0.5 mm.
Dolomite CaMg(COâ)â 96.0â99.0% FeâOâ < 0.1% Used to improve durability; sourced from local quarries.
Feldspar AlâOâ, KâO, NaâO 95.0â99.0% FeâOâ < 0.1% Nigeria, South Africa; used for alumina in container glass.

Source: Glass International, "Raw Materials for the Glass Industry," 2023; Tata Chemicals Magadi, "Soda Ash Product Specification," 2024; BS EN 1051-1:2003.

2. Cullet: Sources, Benefits, and Preparation

Cullet is recycled glass. In Africa, cullet is sourced from bottle collectors, municipal recycling programmes, bottlers' internal returns, and industrial scrap. Cullet reduces furnace energy demand by 2.5â3% per 10% cullet and reduces soda ash and limestone consumption proportionally. However, contaminated cullet (ceramics, metals, organics) causes stones, cords, and colour defects, which are costly in export markets.

Preparation steps: sort by colour, remove ceramics and metals, crush to 10â50 mm, and magnetically separate ferrous metals. For high-quality container glass, cullet should be < 0.5% ceramic and < 0.1% metal.

Table 2: Cullet Quality Grades and Their Business Impact
Grade Ceramic Contamination Metal Contamination Typical Use Price Impact (indicative)
A (Premium) < 0.2% < 0.05% Container glass, tableware Highest; reduces batch cost by 8â12%
B (Standard) 0.2â0.5% 0.05â0.1% Container glass (non-critical) Moderate; reduces batch cost by 5â8%
C (Low) 0.5â1.0% 0.1â0.3% Fibre glass, decorative Low; increases defect risk
D (Reject) > 1.0% > 0.3% Not recommended Negative; causes furnace and quality issues

Source: Glass Technology Services, "Cullet Quality Guidelines," 2022; FEVE, "Cullet Recycling in Europe," 2021 (adapted for African context).

3. Batch Calculation and Mixing Procedures

Batch calculation converts the desired glass oxide composition into raw material weights. For a standard soda-lime-silica container glass, a typical batch (per 1000 kg of glass) is:

  • Silica sand: 600â650 kg
  • Soda ash: 180â200 kg
  • Limestone: 120â150 kg
  • Cullet: 200â400 kg (replacing equivalent raw materials)

When using cullet, reduce soda ash and limestone proportionally. For every 10% cullet added, reduce soda ash by approximately 2% and limestone by 1.5%. Always verify with your furnace supplier's batch formula.

Mixing procedure: Weigh each material separately, then blend in a rotary or paddle mixer for 5â10 minutes. Over-mixing causes segregation of fine and coarse particles; under-mixing causes batch inhomogeneity, leading to cords and stones.

4. Weighing and Blending Equipment

Accurate weighing is the single most important control point. In African plants, common equipment includes:

  • Belt weighers: For continuous sand and cullet feed; accuracy Â±1%.
  • Batch scales: For soda ash and limestone; accuracy Â±0.5%.
  • Rotary mixers: 5â10 minute cycle; 60â80% fill factor.
  • Paddle mixers: For small plants; 3â5 minute cycle.

Calibrate scales weekly. A 1% error in soda ash can shift glass composition by 0.2% NaâO, affecting thermal expansion and forming performance.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING â SILICA DUST AND SODA ASH HAZARDS

Silica sand contains crystalline silica. Prolonged inhalation causes silicosis, an irreversible lung disease. Soda ash is a strong alkali that causes severe eye and skin burns. In African plants where ventilation may be limited:

  • Always wear P2/N95 respirators when handling silica sand or mixing batch.
  • Wear chemical splash goggles and alkali-resistant gloves when handling soda ash.
  • Install local exhaust ventilation at weighing and mixing stations.
  • Never use compressed air to clean silica dust â it re-suspends particles. Use wet methods or vacuum.
  • Provide eyewash stations within 10 seconds' reach of soda ash handling areas.

5. Batch Homogeneity and Quality Control

Batch homogeneity means every 100 g sample of mixed batch has the same chemical composition. Poor homogeneity causes:

  • Stones and cords in finished glass
  • Furnace temperature fluctuations
  • Increased rejection rates (typically 5â15% in African plants)

QC tests:

  • Visual inspection: Check for colour streaks, lumps, and segregation.
  • Sieve analysis: 90% of batch should pass 1 mm; 50% pass 0.5 mm.
  • Chemical analysis: XRF or wet chemistry on random samples; NaâO Â±0.3%, CaO Â±0.2%.
  • Moisture content: Soda ash should be < 0.5% moisture; sand < 0.2%.

6. Storage and Handling of Raw Materials

In Africa's varied climate â from humid coastal zones to dusty Sahelian regions â storage is critical:

  • Silica sand: Store in covered silos or under tarpaulins. Prevent wind-blown dust and rain ingress.
  • Soda ash: Store in sealed bags or silos. Moisture causes caking and inaccurate weighing. Use desiccant bags in humid climates.
  • Limestone: Store in dry, covered areas. Moisture causes lumping.
  • Cullet: Store in covered bunkers. Open storage leads to contamination from leaves, plastics, and metals.

Stock rotation: use FIFO (First In, First Out). Soda ash has a shelf life of 6â12 months in sealed storage; beyond that, caking reduces flowability.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Verify incoming raw material certificates: Check SiOâ, NaâCOâ, CaCOâ purity and FeâOâ content against specification.
  2. Calibrate all scales weekly: Batch scales Â±0.5%, belt weighers Â±1%.
  3. Test cullet contamination: Ceramic < 0.5%, metal < 0.1% for container glass.
  4. Control moisture: Soda ash < 0.5%, sand < 0.2%.
  5. Mix for 5â10 minutes: Check homogeneity by visual and sieve analysis.
  6. Record every batch: Material weights, cullet percentage, mixing time, operator initials.
  7. Inspect storage areas weekly: Check for leaks, moisture, contamination, and pest activity.
  8. Train operators annually: Silica dust and soda ash safety, emergency procedures, and QC protocols.

Further Reading

  • US Glass Manufacturing Industry Council (GMIC) â Raw Materials Resources
  • FEVE â European Container Glass Federation: Cullet Recycling Guidelines
  • Tata Chemicals Magadi â Soda Ash Product Specifications
  • Glass International â Batch House Design and Operation
  • ILO â Safety and Health in the Glass Industry

Business takeaway: In African glass processing, raw material and batch preparation discipline directly determines your cost per tonne and your rejection rate. A 1% improvement in batch accuracy can reduce energy consumption by 0.5â1% and cut defects by 2â3%. Train your batch house team, invest in accurate scales, and source cullet strategically. That is the difference between a profitable plant and a struggling one.

quiz.q: What is the main role of soda ash in a glass batch?
options: A) It adds colour to the glass
B) It lowers the melting point of silica
C) It increases the strength of glass
D) It removes bubbles from the melt
quiz.explanation: Soda ash (sodium carbonate) acts as a flux, reducing the melting temperature of silica from about 1700Â°C to around 1400Â°C.

quiz.q: Which raw material provides calcium oxide (CaO) to make glass more durable?
quiz.explanation: Limestone (calcium carbonate) decomposes to calcium oxide, which improves chemical durability and hardness.

quiz.q: What is a simple field test to check if silica sand has low iron content?
options: A) Burn it and see the colour
B) Put it in water and shake
C) Add vinegar and watch for bubbles
D) Weigh it before and after drying
quiz.explanation: If the water stays clear after shaking sand in a bottle, iron content is likely low; coloured water indicates iron.

quiz.q: Why should you store soda ash in a dry, sealed container?
options: B) It absorbs moisture from the air
quiz.explanation: Soda ash is hygroscopic and clumps when it absorbs moisture, leading to inaccurate weighing.

quiz.q: What is the maximum recommended percentage of cullet in a batch without adding extra soda ash?
quiz.explanation: Using more than 50% cullet can make glass brittle because some oxides are lost; extra soda ash is needed.

quiz.q: Which contaminant in cullet is the most harmful to glass quality?
quiz.explanation: Ceramics do not melt at glass melting temperatures and cause stones or cracks in the final product.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of adding a small amount of water (2-3%) during batch mixing?
options: B) To reduce dust and prevent segregation
quiz.explanation: Water dampens the batch, reducing airborne dust and helping particles stick together to avoid separation.

quiz.q: In batch calculation, if you need 72 kg of SiO2 and your sand is 98% pure, how much sand should you weigh?
quiz.explanation: Weight of sand = 72 / 0.98 = 73.5 kg to supply 72 kg of pure silica.

quiz.q: What is the recommended mixing time for a dry batch in a concrete mixer?
quiz.explanation: Mixing for at least 5 minutes ensures uniform colour and distribution of all ingredients.

quiz.q: Which equipment is essential for accurate batch preparation?
quiz.explanation: A digital scale accurate to 0.1 kg is needed to weigh each raw material correctly.

quiz.q: How often should you calibrate a platform scale used for batch weighing?
quiz.explanation: Weekly calibration with a known weight ensures accuracy and prevents batch errors.

quiz.q: What is a simple test for batch homogeneity?
options: A) Melt samples from different parts and compare
quiz.explanation: Melting samples from top, bottom, and corners and checking for identical colour and clarity shows if mixing is uniform.

quiz.q: If a melted glass sample shows many seeds (bubbles), what is a likely cause?
options: B) Too much moisture or sulphate in batch
quiz.explanation: Excess moisture or sulphate decomposes to produce gas bubbles (seeds) in the melt.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to store cullet?
options: B) In open piles on the ground
C) In covered bins sorted by colour
quiz.explanation: Cullet should be kept dry, covered, and separated by colour to avoid contamination and colour mixing.

quiz.q: Why is it important to use FIFO (first-in, first-out) for raw materials?
options: B) To avoid using old stock that may have degraded
quiz.explanation: Older materials may absorb moisture or cake, affecting batch accuracy and glass quality.

quiz.q: What personal protective equipment (PPE) is essential when handling soda ash?
options: B) Dust mask and safety glasses
quiz.explanation: Soda ash dust irritates eyes and lungs, so a dust mask and safety glasses are necessary.

quiz.q: What is the typical particle size of cullet after crushing for batch use?
quiz.explanation: Cullet is crushed to 10-20 mm for uniform melting and easy mixing.

quiz.q: Which of these is a benefit of using cullet in the batch?
quiz.explanation: Cullet melts at a lower temperature, saving up to 30% fuel and reducing soda ash and limestone needs.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a vibratory screen in batch preparation?
options: B) To remove lumps before mixing
quiz.explanation: A 5 mm mesh screen removes lumps that could cause inhomogeneity or stones in the glass.

quiz.q: How can you check the moisture content of raw materials?
options: B) Dry a sample at 110Â°C for 2 hours and reweigh
quiz.explanation: Oven drying at 110Â°C removes moisture; weight loss gives the moisture percentage.

quiz.q: What is the recommended maximum moisture content for soda ash before weighing?
quiz.explanation: Moisture above 0.5% in soda ash means you must adjust the batch weight to compensate.

quiz.q: Why should you keep a logbook of batch weights and mixing times?
options: B) To trace defects and ensure consistency
quiz.explanation: A logbook helps identify the cause of defects and maintain repeatable quality.

quiz.q: What is a common defect caused by poor mixing (inhomogeneity)?
quiz.explanation: Unmixed batch leads to local variations in composition, causing cords or streaks in the glass.

quiz.q: Which material should be stored on pallets to keep it off the ground?
quiz.explanation: Soda ash bags should be on pallets to prevent moisture absorption from the floor.

quiz.q: What is the approximate cost of a small kiln for test melts mentioned in the lesson?
quiz.explanation: A small kiln for test melts costs about $500 and helps avoid costly production errors.

quiz.q: How can you remove iron contamination from cullet?
quiz.explanation: A magnet attracts iron particles, removing them from the cullet before crushing.

quiz.q: What is the typical batch recipe (by weight) for container glass using local materials?
options: A) 70% sand, 15% soda ash, 10% limestone, 5% cullet
quiz.explanation: A common starting recipe is 70% silica sand, 15% soda ash, 10% limestone, and 5% cullet.

quiz.q: Why is it important to clean a mixer between batches?
quiz.explanation: Leftover batch from a previous mix can alter the composition of the next batch.

quiz.q: What is the first step in preparing cullet for batch use?
quiz.explanation: Sorting by colour is the first step to avoid mixed-colour glass; then remove contaminants, crush, wash, and dry.

quiz.q: What does a clear water test after shaking sand in a bottle indicate?
quiz.explanation: Clear water means iron is low; coloured water means iron is present and may tint the glass.
